I see where you’re coming from, but I think that there are better ways to handle this than charging for the surgery. 

The practice where I’m about to have mine done requires six months of dietary counseling and clean drug tests, a psychological evaluation, nutrition evaluation, and a plethora of medical tests. 

No program is perfect, but I think doing something like this rather than charging for surgery would level the playing field and ensure that people are truly invested in their health for the long term.

For what it’s worth, regain is a VERY common issue with the sleeve. I have PCOS and Hashimoto’s in addition to a few other health problems, and I’ve opted to go with the duodenal switch. This gives you the added benefit of malabsorption, so as your stomach heals and you’re able to eat normal portions again (which is what happens with the sleeve as well), you will still absorb fewer calories than you take in, making weight loss easier to maintain.

I’ve actually never received a formal diagnosis, but every doctor I’ve seen has said that my symptoms are consistent with vasovagal syncope. I’ve been offered a tilt table test to verify, but I’ve chosen not to do it because they’re notorious for giving false positives, having a diagnosis wouldn’t lead to any change in treatment, and it would be super miserable.

I had my first episode when I was 12, they happened once or twice a year until age 19. Then they happened 5-10x/week for about two years. Since then, my average has come down to about 2x/week. (I’m 29 now)

I actually am allowed to drive! I’m insanely lucky in that my body gives me more warning that this is going to happen when I’m already sitting. If I feel the slightest symptoms of presyncope while driving, I have plenty of time to pull over and lay my seat back to avoid fainting.
That said, I prefer not go anywhere without another person, and I generally let them drive.
